summary: Defines a MIB module with managed objects for scheduling management operations to run periodically or at specified dates and times, using SNMP. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: This is an alarm clock for network equipment. You can tell a device to do a chore at a certain time or every so often.

questions: what is the snmp schedule mib
how to schedule snmp set operations
what is the difference between periodic and calendar schedules in snmp
subtitle: A standard SNMP table that lets a device run management actions on a timer or at set dates and times.

tldr.problem: Network managers want devices to perform management operations periodically or at specific times, such as turning an interface off on weekends, without a manager having to send each command at the right moment.
tldr.mechanism: The Schedule MIB defines a table of schedules. Each row has a timing rule (periodic, calendar or one-shot) and an action, which is an SNMP set of an integer value on a local MIB variable.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3231 obsoletes RFC 2591. It adds the schedTriggers counter, clarifies behavior and deprecates the older compliance and group definitions.

today: RFC 3231 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2591. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: What the Schedule MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 3231 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for network management protocols. Its objects schedule management operations periodically or at specified dates and times. The actions can realize on-duty / off-duty schedules or trigger management functions in a distributed management application.

Schedules can be enabled or disabled by changing a control object, so pre-configured schedules can be switched on or off by some other management function. The memo uses the word scheduler for the entity that implements the MIB and invokes the actions at the right times.

The module is written in SMIv2. The RFC also describes the SNMP Management Framework it belongs to, and says a MIB conforming to SMIv1 can be produced through the appropriate translations.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a list of reminders inside a network device. Each reminder says what to do and when to do it.

sections.title: Periodic, Calendar and One-shot Schedules
sections.content:
A periodic schedule is a fixed number of seconds between the start of one action and the start of the next. The time the action takes is usually unknown to the scheduler and does not change the next scheduling point. Implementations must guarantee that an invocation does not happen before its scheduled time, but they may delay it under local constraints such as heavy load. Accumulated delays that make the interval drift should be avoided.

A calendar schedule fires on chosen months, days, weekdays, hours and minutes. Several values can be set for each item. Bits within one item are combined with OR, and the different items are combined with AND. For example, june and july in schedMonth with monday and friday in schedWeekDay means every Monday and Friday in June and July. Setting all bits wildcards an item. A schedule that can never fire, such as one for February 31st, is simply ignored. Calendar schedules use local time, which a manager can read from schedLocalTime together with the offset to GMT.

A one-shot schedule is like a calendar schedule, except that it disables itself after it has invoked an action.
sections.plainLanguage: A periodic schedule is like brushing your teeth every day. A calendar schedule is like a birthday on a fixed date. A one-shot schedule is an alarm that rings once and then switches itself off.

sections.title: Actions and Time Transitions
sections.content:
A scheduled action is an SNMP set operation on a local MIB variable, and only variables of type INTEGER are allowed. That is enough for simple on-duty / off-duty schedules on resources with a status object such as ifAdminStatus. For more complex work, an action can start a management script, which can in turn do SNMP set operations on remote SNMP engines.

A time transition happens when the clock reported by schedLocalTime loses continuity, for example because of daylight savings time or an administrative change. If time is set backwards, some times occur twice (ambiguous times), and an action scheduled at such a time is invoked at every occurrence. If time is set forwards, some times never occur (nonexistent times), and an action scheduled at such a time is not invoked at all.

The RFC's example: an action set for 2:10 am runs twice if the clock is set back from 3:00 am to 2:00 am, and does not run if the clock jumps from 2:00 am to 3:00 am.
sections.plainLanguage: When clocks change for daylight saving, an hour can happen twice or be skipped. A chore set for a repeated hour is done twice, and a chore set for a skipped hour is not done.

sections.title: The Schedule Table
sections.content:
The module is DISMAN-SCHEDULE-MIB, placed at mib-2 63. Its main object is schedTable, indexed by schedOwner (up to 32 characters, with meaning set by the security policy) and schedName (1 to 32 characters, locally unique).

Each row holds the timing rule and the action:

  • schedType selects periodic, calendar or oneshot. schedInterval gives the seconds for periodic schedules, and a value of 0 means the schedule never fires.
  • schedWeekDay, schedMonth, schedDay, schedHour and schedMinute are BITS objects for calendar schedules. schedDay counts days from the start of the month with the d bits and from the end with the r bits.
  • schedVariable, schedContextName and schedValue name the local variable, its context and the integer written to it.
  • schedAdminStatus is the desired state, schedOperStatus the actual one (enabled, disabled or finished), and schedRowStatus and schedStorageType manage the row.

Status objects report failures: schedFailures, schedLastFailure, schedLastFailed and the new schedTriggers, which counts all attempts to invoke the action, successful or not. A schedActionFailure notification is generated whenever an invocation fails.
sections.plainLanguage: The table is a notebook with one page per chore. Each page says when to do the chore, what to change, whether the chore is switched on, and whether it has gone wrong lately.

sections.title: Usage Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives three worked configurations. The first starts a script every 20 minutes to ping devices, using schedInterval = 1200 with a periodic schedule. The second starts a script on the next Friday the 13th at midnight with a calendar-style one-shot schedule that sets every month, the day bit d13, the weekday friday, hour h0 and minute m0.

The third turns a network interface off on Friday evening at 20:30 and back on Monday morning at 5:30. Two calendar schedules write the values down(2) and up(1) to ifAdminStatus.6. The RFC adds that similar entries could enable and disable the periodic schedule from the first example.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show how to set the alarm clock to ping machines often, to run a script on Friday the 13th, and to switch a network connection off for the weekend.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with read-write or read-create access may be sensitive, and SET operations without proper protection can hurt network operations. SNMPv1 by itself is not secure, so implementers should consider SNMPv3, specifically the User-based Security Model and the View-based Access Control Model.

Scheduled sets must use the security credentials that were present when the row was created, so an implementation must record them for every entry. Access control rules must be applied when the set is done, through the isAccessAllowed service from RFC 2571, with the write view.

Actions are limited to the local MIB, which avoids problems with delegating access rights. A user could still own schedules that trigger far in the future, so entries in schedTable SHOULD be cleaned up whenever a user is removed from an SNMP engine. The initial index, schedOwner, serves as an owner index that can be mapped to a security name in VACM.
sections.plainLanguage: A scheduled chore must be done with the same permissions as the person who set it up. If that person leaves, their old alarms should be thrown away.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 2591
sections.content:
This memo is a revision of RFC 2591. The main changes were:

  • The framework text and references were updated, and revision clauses were added to the module identity.
  • Time transitions were clarified, as was the rule that schedInterval and the calendar objects can be modified whatever the row, admin and operational status are.
  • Implementations must re-calculate pending invocations when scheduling parameters change, schedOperStatus must not be enabled while schedRowStatus is not active, and the access check can be delegated by sending the SNMP Set to oneself.
  • The schedTriggers object was added, defaults were added for schedContextName, schedVariable and schedValue, and the old schedCompliance and schedGroup were deprecated in favor of schedCompliance2 and schedGroup2.
sections.plainLanguage: This edition fixes confusing spots in the old one and adds a counter for how many times each alarm went off.

items.label: periodic
items.desc: Runs every schedInterval seconds; calendar bits are ignored.

items.label: calendar
items.desc: Runs at local times matching the weekday, month, day, hour and minute bits.

items.label: oneshot
items.desc: Like calendar, but moves to finished after its first action.
